clue.text: In which one gets time to check mate?

definitions.text: In which one gets time to check mate?

parts.words: In which one gets time to check mate?
parts.note: reads like a chess problem about time to deliver checkmate, but 'mate' is a partner and 'check' means test out before committing to wedlock

explanation.surface: A chess player wonders which position allows time to deliver checkmate.
explanation.walkthrough: The chess words 'check' and 'mate' pull towards the board; really a couple tries living as husband and wife for a period before deciding to wed.
explanation.definitionFit: A trial period of living together lets someone test a prospective spouse before a permanent commitment.

clue.text: He should be fair, but he doesn't play the game

definitions.text: He should be fair, but he doesn't play the game

parts.words: He should be fair, but he doesn't play the game
parts.note: 'doesn't play the game' sounds like cheating, but literally this official takes no part in the match he oversees impartially

explanation.surface: A complaint about someone who ought to be honest yet behaves unsportingly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doesn't play the game' idiomatically means behaving dishonourably; read literally, it describes the match official who judges but never plays.
explanation.definitionFit: A sports umpire must be impartial and enforces the rules without being one of the players.

clue.text: Hairstyle for a makeover

indicators.note: a makeover remodels something, so the letters of the words before it are rebuilt in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone asks for a hairstyle suited to a beauty makeover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'makeover' rearranges FORA into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A rounded, bushy natural hairdo is one style of hair.

clue.text: "Pass him, anyway" — how accidents are caused

indicators.note: 'anyway' here means in any old way, so the letters of the quoted words are set down in another order

explanation.surface: A driver is urged to overtake regardless, which is how crashes happen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anyway' rearranges PASSHIM; 'how ... are caused' just links the quotation to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Mishaps are unlucky incidents, a milder synonym for accidents.

clue.text: Frauds seen in court or in the press

definitions.text: seen in court or in the press
definitions.meaning: the bats used in squash or tennis appear on a court, and are kept in a press to stop warping

explanation.surface: Swindles exposed in legal proceedings or newspaper reports.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Court' and 'press' suggest law and journalism; they are a squash court and the wooden frame that keeps strung bats flat.
explanation.definitionFit: Swindling schemes are called this, and so are the strung bats used in tennis and squash.

clue.text: It has no earthly connection with the mainland

definitions.text: It has no earthly connection with the mainland

parts.words: It has no earthly connection with the mainland
parts.note: 'no earthly connection' sounds like 'nothing whatsoever to do with', but literally there is no land bridge, only water

explanation.surface: Something is said to be entirely unrelated to the mainland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No earthly' is idiom for 'not the slightest'; read literally, no earth joins this piece of land to the continent.
explanation.definitionFit: A small island is surrounded by sea, with no land link to the continent.

clue.text: Attempt with catapult to get a young bird

parts.note: a go is a try or attempt
a sling is a simple catapult for hurling stones

explanation.surface: A boy tries a catapult to bring down a young bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A gosling is a baby goose, a young waterfowl.

clue.text: Complete course for drivers

parts.note: suggests a full driving-school programme, but the drivers are golf clubs and the course is a golf links played in full

explanation.surface: An advertisement for a full training programme for motorists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drivers' suggests motorists; in golf a driver is the club for long tee shots, and a full round is played over this many greens.
explanation.definitionFit: A standard full round of golf covers that number of greens on the links.

clue.text: Little wonder

parts.note: sounds like the phrase 'no surprise', but means a marvel who is small, that is, a very gifted young child

explanation.surface: A shrug: it is hardly surprising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little wonder' usually means 'unsurprisingly'; here it is literally a wonder who is little, a remarkably talented child.
explanation.definitionFit: A child genius, such as the young Mozart, is a small marvel of talent.

clue.text: Shops for peachs

definitions.meaning: to shop someone is British slang for betraying them to the police
to peach is an old word for turning informer; printed here without its usual E

explanation.surface: A list entry offering shops in exchange for peaches.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words look like nouns (stores, fruit) but are verbs: 'shop' and 'peach' both mean to tell tales on someone to the authorities.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are slang verbs for betraying a person to the police by telling on them.

clue.text: Visits, but speaks without entering?

definitions.meaning: drops by, pays a call on someone
telephones a workplace or radio show, phoning in rather than turning up

explanation.surface: Someone pays a visit yet talks from the doorstep without coming inside.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase means both dropping in on someone and phoning in, for instance to a radio programme or to report sick.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means paying a visit and also telephoning an organisation rather than going there.

clue.text: Cape being blown in the wind?

definitions.meaning: the headland at the southern tip of South America
a brass instrument blown in the orchestra's wind section

explanation.surface: A cloak flapping about in a gale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cape' looks like a cloak and 'wind' like weather; one is Cape Horn, the other the wind section of an orchestra.
explanation.definitionFit: The southern tip of Chile is called Cape Horn, and the brass instrument of that name is played by blowing.

clue.text: Bags of patients

definitions.meaning: doctors refer to individual patients as instances of illness

explanation.surface: Lots of people under medical care.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bags of' reads as slang for 'lots of'; split, 'Bags' is luggage and 'patients' are a doctor's medical files.
explanation.definitionFit: Suitcases are luggage, and a doctor speaks of each patient treated as one such instance.

clue.text: There's a marked inclination here to knock back a drink

indicators.note: to knock back a drink is to down it, and here it turns the words before it backwards

parts.note: a sip is a small drink

explanation.surface: A bar-room remark about someone fond of downing a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knock back' reverses ASIP. The definition refers to the famous Leaning Tower in this Italian city.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian city is famous for its leaning bell tower, a pronounced tilt.

clue.text: Descriptive of a great sea-power

parts.note: sounds like a navy-dominant nation, but means the energy of the sea's rise and fall

explanation.surface: A history book's adjective for a dominant naval nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sea-power' suggests a nation with a strong navy; literally it is the power of the sea, harnessed by barrages from the ebb and flow.
explanation.definitionFit: Electricity generated by the rise and fall of the ocean is given this adjective.

clue.text: Desist from mounting watch?

indicators.note: in a down clue mounting means climbing, so the word for watch is read from bottom to top

parts.note: a timer is a watch or clock used to time things

explanation.surface: A guard is told to stop climbing up to keep watch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mounting' reverses TIMER in this down clue. 'Remit' in the sense of 'desist from' is a dated use, like remitting one's efforts.
explanation.definitionFit: To remit an effort is to slacken or give it up, an old sense of ceasing.

clue.text: The converse of friends

parts.note: 'converse' looks like conversation among friends, but means the opposite

explanation.surface: A description of friends chatting together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Converse' as a noun can mean talk; here it means the reverse, the opposite of friends.
explanation.definitionFit: Foes are the opposite of allies, those hostile rather than friendly.

clue.text: Cunning action made with the French in view

indicators.note: one piece goes in the other, the French article sitting inside the word for view

parts.note: sight means a view, something seen
le is French for the

explanation.surface: A crafty move is made in full sight of the French.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' places LE inside SIGHT. The answer is the trickery of a conjuror's hand.
explanation.definitionFit: A deft trick, as in sleight of hand, is skilful deceptive dexterity.

clue.text: Certainly less than 50%

definitions.meaning: an emphatic British yes, meaning 'very much so'

explanation.surface: Someone assures us a share is definitely under fifty per cent.
explanation.walkthrough: As a British exclamation the phrase means 'absolutely!'; taken literally it means falling short of one half.
explanation.definitionFit: The British exclamation means 'very much so', and literally it describes a share below a half.

clue.text: New coat? Yes, put on for warmth

indicators.note: new signals a fresh arrangement of the letters in the next two words

explanation.surface: Someone agrees to wear a new coat to keep warm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' rearranges COATYES. The definition is a description: the thing placed over a teapot to keep it hot.
explanation.definitionFit: The padded cover goes over a teapot to keep the brew hot.

clue.text: A zealot — in fact, a loony

indicators.note: loony means crazy, so the letters before it are jumbled into a mad order

explanation.surface: Someone declares that a zealot is in truth a lunatic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loony' rearranges INFACTA.
explanation.definitionFit: A fanatic is an extreme enthusiast, someone obsessively devoted to a cause.

clue.text: Artist keeps a boat by the bank

definitions.text: keeps a boat by the bank
definitions.meaning: a rope at the bow used to tie a small boat to a mooring

explanation.surface: An artist moors a boat beside the riverbank.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is nautical: the line attached to a dinghy's bow for tying it up.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is a picture-maker; the other is the bow rope that ties a dinghy to a mooring.

clue.text: In high spirits — because of full pay settlement?

indicators.note: a settlement is a resolution, here of the letters of the words before it into a new order

explanation.surface: Workers cheerful after a pay deal gives them full wages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'settlement' rearranges FULLPAY.
explanation.definitionFit: Being frisky and fun-loving is another way of being in good spirits.

clue.text: Worst place in motor-racing?

parts.note: the slang for the worst possible state, literally the service areas by the racetrack

explanation.surface: A question about the lowest position in a motor race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worst place' suggests last in the race; the phrase is slang for the absolute worst, and also the trackside refuelling bays.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for the very worst, it also names the service bays where racing cars stop for tyres and fuel.

clue.text: Shape of eggs at first light

parts.note: ova are eggs, the Latin plural of ovum

indicators.note: at first takes only the opening letter of the word light

explanation.surface: Describing how eggs look at dawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at first' gives L from 'light'.
explanation.definitionFit: An oval is an egg-like elongated round figure.

clue.text: Some of the main castles conquered by Spain

indicators.note: Some of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Several of the chief castles fell to Spanish conquest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some of' points to the run inside 'maIN CASTLES'. The definition describes the Andean empire's people defeated by Pizarro.
explanation.definitionFit: The Andean empire of Peru fell to Spanish conquistadors under Pizarro in the 1530s.

clue.text: Drop of moisture round bearing is not good

indicators.note: round means the word for not good goes around the bearing

parts.note: bad means not good
E, east, is a compass bearing

explanation.surface: A drop of water around a machine bearing is a bad sign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' puts BAD around E. 'Bearing' suggests machinery; it is a compass direction.
explanation.definitionFit: A bead of sweat or dew is a small rounded droplet.

clue.text: Small photograph and article set in type

parts.note: pic is a short word for a picture
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A small photo and a story are set in print for the paper.
explanation.walkthrough: Pica is a printers' size of type, about one sixth of an inch.
explanation.definitionFit: Pica is a traditional size of printing letter, twelve points.

clue.text: Bar parlour where bangers are served up

indicators.note: in a down clue served up means brought upwards, so the word for bangers reads from the bottom

parts.note: guns go bang, so they are bangers

explanation.surface: A pub's back room where sausages are on the menu.
explanation.walkthrough: 'served up' reverses GUNS. Bangers look like British sausages; here they are things that go bang. A snug is a small cosy room in a British pub.
explanation.definitionFit: A snug is a small private room in a British pub, a cosy bar parlour.

clue.text: He and I are inseparable

parts.note: sounds like two close friends, but describes a person who can never separate himself from 'I', always talking about himself

explanation.surface: Someone describes a close bond with a friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He and I' suggests two pals; it is one man who never stops thinking about himself, so he and the word 'I' are never apart.
explanation.definitionFit: A self-centred person is constantly preoccupied with himself and his own ego.

clue.text: Sport enclosure

definitions.meaning: the sport of swordplay with foils, épées and sabres
a barrier of posts and rails round a field

explanation.surface: A sports ground with a boundary.
explanation.definitionFit: Swordplay as a sport and a barrier around land share this name.

clue.text: Deliveryman?

parts.note: suggests someone who brings parcels, but the deliveries are of babies by a women's-health doctor

explanation.surface: A courier who drops off parcels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deliveryman' suggests a parcel courier; this specialist in women's health may deliver babies.
explanation.definitionFit: A doctor specialising in women's reproductive health may also help bring babies into the world.
